headings.title: Introduction to Anatomy and Physiology
headings.content: Understanding the human body begins with two foundational sciences: **anatomy** and **physiology**. Anatomy studies the structure of body parts and their physical relationships to one another. For example, a nurse looks at the macroscopic anatomy of the arm when palpating a brachial pulse. Physiology examines how these body parts function and carry out the life-sustaining activities of the human organism. While anatomy provides the static blueprint of the body, physiology reveals its dynamic, working mechanisms. Structure always determines function; the delicate, thin walls of the air sacs in the lungs allow for the rapid diffusion of oxygen, perfectly matching their job of gas exchange.

headings.title: Levels of Structural Organization
headings.content:
The human body is organized in a hierarchical structure, scaling up from microscopic building blocks to complex systems:

- **Chemical level**: The simplest level, consisting of atoms and molecules like water, glucose, and proteins.
- **Cellular level**: The basic structural and functional units of life, such as smooth muscle cells or neurons.
- **Tissue level**: Groups of similar cells working together to perform a specific function, including epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous tissues.
- **Organ level**: Structures composed of two or more tissue types that perform a recognized, specialized function, like the stomach or heart.
- **Organ system level**: Groups of organs that cooperate to accomplish a common purpose, such as the digestive or cardiovascular system.
- **Organismal level**: The highest level, representing the complete, living human being composed of all working systems.

headings.title: Characteristics of Living Human Organisms
headings.content: To maintain life, the human body must perform several essential life processes. **Metabolism** encompasses all chemical reactions occurring within body cells, combining catabolism (breaking down substances) and anabolism (building up structures). **Responsiveness** is the ability to sense changes in the internal or external environment and react to them, such as pulling a hand away from a hot stove. **Movement** includes not only walking and running, but also the propulsion of blood, food, and urine through internal tracts. Other vital processes include **growth**, **reproduction**, and **differentiation**, where unspecialized cells develop into specialized forms.

headings.title: Anatomical Terminology and Body Planes
headings.content:
Precise medical language prevents confusion when describing body locations. In the standard **anatomical position**, the person stands upright, feet flat on the floor, arms at the sides, and palms facing forward. 

Body planes create flat surfaces that slice the body to reveal internal structures:
- **Sagittal plane**: Divides the body vertically into right and left parts. A median or midsagittal plane cuts directly down the exact midline.
- **Frontal (coronal) plane**: Divides the body vertically into anterior (front) and posterior (back) portions.
- **Transverse plane**: Divides the body horizontally into superior (upper) and inferior (lower) areas, creating cross-sections.

headings.title: Body Cavities and Membranes
headings.content:
The body is internally partitioned into enclosed spaces called cavities that protect delicate organs. The **dorsal body cavity** protects the nervous system and contains the cranial cavity (brain) and the vertebral canal (spinal cord). The larger **ventral body cavity** houses internal visceral organs and is subdivided into the thoracic cavity and the abdominopelvic cavity by the diaphragm.

Membranes line these closed cavities and the organs within them. The walls of the ventral cavity and the outer surfaces of internal organs are covered by a double-layered serous membrane. The parietal layer lines the cavity wall, while the visceral layer folds inward to cover the organ itself. A slippery lubricating fluid between these layers reduces friction as organs move and change shape.

headings.title: Homeostasis and Control Systems
headings.content:
Homeostasis is the body's ability to maintain a relatively stable internal environment despite continuous external changes. Regulation is achieved through continuous feedback loops. A **receptor** monitors changes and sends information to the **control center**, which determines the set point and sends signals to an **effector**. 

Most homeostatic control mechanisms use **negative feedback** to shut off or reduce the original stimulus, such as when shivering generates heat to reverse a drop in body temperature. Conversely, **positive feedback** mechanisms enhance or accelerate the original stimulus, driving the process to a rapid conclusion, such as uterine contractions during childbirth.
